Paleomagnetism and rock magnetism of early Cretaceous Rajmahal basalts,
T
NE India: Implications for paleogeography of the Indian subcontinent and
migration of the Kerguelen hotspot
⁎
M.R. Kapawar, Venkateshwarlu Mamilla
CSIR- National Geophysical Research Institute, Hyderabad-500007, India
ARTICLE INFO ABSTRACT
Keywords: We present here new paleomagnetic and rock magnetic results from Rajmahal Traps (RT), India. The results are
Paleomagnetism comprising of 350 standard specimens collected from 18 sites (90 samples). The detailed rock magnetic studies
Rock magnetism indicate that a Single Domain (SD) magnetite [Fe3O4] is the dominant magnetic carrier with ilmenite, pyrrhotite,
Rajmahal Traps and maghemite in the accessory form. The calculated Characteristic Remanent Magnetization (ChRM) directions
Kerguelen hotspot
APWP
yield a mean declination of 317.51°; mean inclination of −61.92° (α95 = 3.6°; k = 93.39). The obtained Virtual
Geomagnetic Pole (VGP) position of the RT at ~117 Ma is 11.37°N, 297.58°E (62.42°W) with A95 = 3.5°,
Paleogeographic position
k = 99.99, dp = 4.33, dm = 5.58, and the calculated paleolatitude is at 43.1°S indistinguishable from that of
earlier works. This paleomagnetic pole of RT basalts has minimal effect of secular variation and comply with the
Geocentric Axial Dipole (GAD) model. The VGP is plotted on synthetic Apparent Polar Wander Path (APWP) for
India, constrained better, and agrees well with the previously reported poles. The postulation of migration of
mantle plume and the global mantle circulations are tested, and the present study results are in accord with this,
suggesting the southward migration of the Kerguelen hotspot (mantle plume) by at least 6°.

4.2.2. Hysteresis loop study
The magnetic hysteresis loop analysis was conducted on 18 samples.
The magnetic hysteresis loops obtained for these samples are presented
in Fig. 5. The samples with different mineral assemblages and dissimilar
grain sizes showcase different shapes of magnetic hysteresis loops.
Further, the remanence ratio (Mrs/Ms) and coercivity ratio (Hcr/Hc)
were determined from the hysteresis parameters of saturation magne-
tization (Ms), saturation remanence (Mrs), coercivity force (Hc) and
coercivity remanence (Hcr), and summarised in table 2. These ratios
(Mrs/Ms versus Hcr/Hc) are plotted on a ‘Day plot’ (Day et al., 1977),
shown in Fig. 6. This Day plot specifies and distinguishes the Single
Domain (SD), Pseudo-Single Domain (PSD), and Multidomain (MD)
magnetic grains and will also serve as a better magnetic granulometry

Overall, the main magnetic carrier identified in our study is the
ferrimagnetic magnetite and other minerals, like ilmenite, pyrrhotite,
and maghemite, revealing their accessory occurrence in the samples.
Identifying these magnetic minerals in RT basalts may allow us to use
mineral alteration as a reference for further studies concentrating on

### page_7
M.R. Kapawar and V. Mamilla Journal of Asian Earth Sciences 201 (2020) 104517
Whereas in the present study, we have collected samples from the same
area (RT 5), which show a clear normal polarity direction (D = 346°,
I = -67°), so there ends the doubt of the presence of reversed polarity in
this area. However, Das et al. (1996) have reported a brief reversal
event in the Hetbanda section of RT basalts, which he claims as to the
commencement of trap emplacement. From our results, it is established
that the basalts with normal polarity exist in the northern parts of RT.
5.2. Paleogeography of the Indian subcontinent
The paleogeography of the Indian subcontinent has been attempted
by assessing the volcanic outputs left on the Indian Plate by the Indian
Ocean hotspots. The Indian Ocean has mainly four hotspots (plume
heads), the Kerguelen, Reunion, Marion, and Crozet. The present study
concerns with a volcanic product of the Kerguelen hotspot, i.e.,
Rajmahal basalts. The Rajmahal basalts of the Indian subcontinent and
the Bunbury basalts of the Australian Plate (Olierook et al., 2016) has
preserved the geological connectivity between these two continental
plates and suggest their genesis through a single parental hotspot, i.e.,
the Kerguelen hotspot. It indicates that Indian and Australian plates
were nearby when these rock units were emplaced on respective plates
due to initial Kerguelen volcanic activity. At ~ 117 Ma, the RT was
formed over the eastern margin of India due to Kerguelen hotspot ac-
Fig. 6. The hysteresis parameters, Mrs/ Ms and Hcr/ Hc are plotted on a Day
tivity (Courtillot, 1999; Coffin et al., 2002; Kent et al., 2002; Ghatak
plot (Day et al., 1977) with the theoretical SD-MD and SP-SD mixing lines from
and Basu, 2013). Most of the northern Indian rocks are either eroded/
Dunlop (2002).
buried under extensive alluvium cover or are disturbed due to orogeny
and the Himalayan subduction mechanism. Hence, the RT becomes a
the geological processes. The rock magnetic properties of the RT basalts
suitable candidate for study to decipher the Indian subcontinent pa-

leogeographic position during the early Cretaceous period.
controlled by the cooling history of lava.

better define the paleogeographic position of the Indian Plate (Fig. 8a),
